readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|The deer was flying through the park, followed by the ''whirlwind'' of hounds and hunters.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xxi.}}}}

'''To sow the wind and reap the whirlwind.''' See ''wind''<sup>2</sup>.

'''whirl-worm''' (hwėrl′wėrm), ''n.'' A turbellarian; any member of the ''Turbellaria''.

'''whirly-bat†''' (hwėr′li-bat), ''n.'' Same as ''whirl-bat''.
{{smaller block|Very true, and he also propos’d the fighting with ''Whirly-bats'' too, and I don’t like that Sport.
{{right|''N. Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 84.}}}}

'''whirret†''' (hwir′et), ''n.'' [Perhaps from ''whir''.] A slap; a blow. Also written ''wherret'', ''whirrit'', ''whirrick''.
{{smaller block|<poem>And in a fume gave Furius
A ''whirret'' on the eare.</poem>
{{right|''Kendall'', Flowers of Epigrams (1577). (''Nares''.)}}
I forthwith went, he following me at my heels, and now and then giving me a ''whirret'' on the ear, which, the way to my chamber lying through the hall where John Raunce was, he, poor man, might see and be sorry for, as I doubt not that he was, but could not help me.
{{right|''T. Ellwood'', Life (ed. Howells), p. 222.}}
<poem>Then there’s your souse, your ''wherrit'', and your dowst,
Tugs on the hair, your bob o’ the lips,—a whelp on ’t!
I ne’er could find much difference.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Nice Valour, iii. 2.}}}}

'''whirret†''' (hwir′et), ''v. t.'' [Also ''wherret'', etc.; cf. ''whirret'', ''n.''] '''1.''' To hurry; trouble; tease. ''Bickerstaff'', Love in a Village, i. 5.—'''2.''' To give a box on the ear to. ''Beau. and Fl.''

¶
'''whirrick''' (hwir′ik), ''n.'' A variant of ''whirret.''
{{smaller block|Harry . . . gave master such a ''whirrick!''
{{right|''H. Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 21. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''whirrit†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''whirret.''

'''whirry''' (hwėr′i), ''v.'' [A dial. form of ''whir'' or of ''hurry.''] '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To fly rapidly with noise; whir; hurry.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To hurry. [Scotch in both uses.]

'''whirtle''' (hwėr′tl), ''n.'' [Origin obscure.] A perforated steel plate through which pipe or wire is drawn to reduce its diameter. ''E. H. Knight.''

'''whish<sup>1</sup>''' (hwish), ''v. i.'' [Imitative; cf. ''whiz'' and ''swish.''] To move with the whirring or whizzing sound of rapid motion.
{{smaller block|The scenery of a long tragic drama flashed through his mind as the lightning-express train ''whishes'' by a station.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, vi.}}}}

'''whish<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwish), ''interj.'' [Var. of ''hush.''] Hush.
{{smaller block|<poem>What means this peevish babe? ''Whish'', lullaby;
What ails my babe? what ails my babe to cry?</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, ii. 8.}}}}

'''whish<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwish), ''a.'' [Var. of ''hush.''] Silent: same as ''hush'', ''whisht'', ''whist''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|You took my answer well, and all was ''whish.''
{{right|''Sir J. Harington'', Ep., i. 27.}}}}

'''whishey, whishie''' (hwish′i), ''n.'' The whitethroat, ''Sylvia cinerea. Macgillivray.'' Also ''whattie.''

'''whisht†''' (hwisht), ''interj.'' and ''v.'' [Var. of ''husht.''] Same as ''husht'', ''whist''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|When they perceived that Solomon, by the advise of his father, was annoynted king, by and by there was all ''whisht.''
{{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}}

<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|whirlpit|6905|whiskered}}</noinclude>{{nop}}'''whirlpit†''' (hwėrl′pit), ''n.''   [< ''whirl'' + ''pit''<sup>1</sup>.]   A whirlpool.
{{smaller block|The deepest ''whirl-pit'' of the rav’nous seas.
{{right|''B. Jonson'', Every Man out of his Humour, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|This ''whirle-pit'' is said to have thrown up her wracks neer Tauromenia.
{{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 192.}}}}

'''whirlpool''' (hwėrl′pöl), ''n.''   [Early mod. E. ''whirlpoole'', ''whirlpole''; < ''whirl'' + ''pool''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' A circular eddy or current in a river or the sea produced by the configuration of the channel, by meeting currents, by winds meeting tides, etc. {{smaller|The celebrated whirlpool of Charybdis between Sicily and Italy, and the Maelstrom off the coast of Norway, are not whirlpools in the strict sense, but merely superficial commotions caused by winds meeting tidal currents, and in calm weather are free from danger. Instances of vertical motion, however, do occur, as in the whirlpool of Coryvreckan in the Hebrides, between Jura and Scarba, and in some eddies among the Orkneys.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Greedy ''Whirl-pools'', ever-wheeling round,
Suck in, at once, Oars, Sails, and Ships to ground.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Battle of Ivry.}}}}

'''2†.''' Some huge sea-monster of the whale kind; a whirl-whale; a whirl-about.
{{smaller block|The Indian Sea breedeth the most and the biggest fishes that are; among which the whales and ''whirlpools'', called balænæ, take up in length as much as four acres or arpens of land.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, i. 235. (''Trench.'')}}}}

'''whirl-puff†''' (hwėrl′puf), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whirlpuff''; < ''whirl'' + ''puff''.]   A whirlwind.   ''Wyclif.''
{{smaller block|A ''whirle-puffe'' or ghust called Typhen.
{{right|''Holland'', tr. of Pliny, ii. 48.}}}}

'''whirlwater†''' (hwėrl′wâ″tėr), ''n.'' An old name for a waterspout.
{{smaller block|There was no other water fell over the duke’s water-gate than what came of the breaking there of the ''whirlwater'', or, as some call it, the water-pillar.
{{right|''Court and Times of Charles I.'', I. 114.}}}}

'''whirl-whale†''' (hwėrl′hwāl), ''n.'' A monster of the whale kind; a whirl-about; a whirlpool.
{{smaller block|<poem>Another, swallowed in a ''Whirl-Whales'' womb,
Is laid a-live within a living Toomb.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, ii., The Lawe.}}}}

'''whirlwig''' (hwėrl′wig), ''n.''   [A var. of ''whirlgig'', perhaps simulating ''-wig'' in ''earwig''.]   Same as ''whirligig'', 4.

'''whirlwind''' (hwėrl′wind), ''n.''   [< ME. ''whyrlewynde'', ''qwirl-wind'', a whirling wind, = D. ''wervelwind'' = G. ''wirbelwind'' = Icel. ''hvirfilvindr'' = Sw. ''hvirfvelvind'' = Dan. ''hvirvelvind'', a whirlwind; as ''whirl'' + ''wind''<sup>2</sup>, ''n.'']   '''1.''' A wind moving in a circumscribed circular path; a mass of air, of which the height is generally very great in comparison with its width, rotating rapidly round a vertical or slightly inclined axis, this axis having at the same time a progressive motion over the surface of the land or sea. {{smaller|Whirlwinds vary greatly in dimensions and intensity, the term including the miniature eddy that circles in the dusty street, the towering sand-pillars of the tropical deserts, the waterspout formed over bodies of water, and the destructive tornado of the United States. They arise when the atmosphere is in a condition of instability, and are one of the processes by which a stable condition is regained.}}
{{smaller block|The Lord answered Job out of the ''whirlwind''.
{{right|Job xxxviii. 1.}}}}
'''2.''' Figuratively, any wild circling rush resembling a whirlwind.
{{smaller block|<poem>There the companions of his fall, o’erwhelm’d
With floods and ''whirlwinds'' of tempestuous fire,
He soon discerns.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., i. 77.}}}}
{{smaller block|What a ''whirlwind'' is her head!
{{right|''Byron.''}}}}

{{smaller block|The deer was flying through the park, followed by the ''whirlwind'' of hounds and hunters.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xxi.}}}}

'''To sow the wind and reap the whirlwind.''' See ''wind''<sup>2</sup>.

'''whirl-worm''' (hwėrl′wėrm), ''n.'' A turbellarian; any member of the ''Turbellaria''.

'''whirly-bat†''' (hwėr′li-bat), ''n.'' Same as ''whirl-bat''.
{{smaller block|Very true, and he also propos’d the fighting with ''Whirly-bats'' too, and I don’t like that Sport.
{{right|''N. Bailey'', tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 84.}}}}

'''whirret†''' (hwir′et), ''n.''   [Perhaps from ''whir''.]   A slap; a blow. Also written ''wherret'', ''whirrit'', ''whirrick''.
{{smaller block|<poem>And in a fume gave Furius
A ''whirret'' on the eare.</poem>
{{right|''Kendall'', Flowers of Epigrams (1577). (''Nares''.)}}}}
{{smaller block|I forthwith went, he following me at my heels, and now and then giving me a ''whirret'' on the ear, which, the way to my chamber lying through the hall where John Raunce was, he, poor man, might see and be sorry for, as I doubt not that he was, but could not help me.
{{right|''T. Ellwood'', Life (ed. Howells), p. 222.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Then there’s your souse, your ''wherrit'', and your dowst,
Tugs on the hair, your bob o’ the lips,—a whelp on ’t!
I ne’er could find much difference.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Nice Valour, iii. 2.}}}}

'''whirret†''' (hwir′et), ''v. t.''   [Also ''wherret'', etc.; cf. ''whirret'', ''n.'']   '''1.''' To hurry; trouble; tease.   ''Bickerstaff'', Love in a Village, i. 5.—'''2.''' To give a box on the ear to.   ''Beau. and Fl.''

'''whirrick''' (hwir′ik), ''n.'' A variant of ''whirret.''
{{smaller block|Harry . . . gave master such a ''whirrick!''
{{right|''H. Brooke'', Fool of Quality, I. 21. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''whirrit†''', ''n.'' and ''v.'' See ''whirret.''

'''whirry''' (hwėr′i), ''v.''   [A dial. form of ''whir'' or of ''hurry.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' To fly rapidly with noise; whir; hurry.

'''II.''' ''trans.'' To hurry. [Scotch in both uses.]

'''whirtle''' (hwėr′tl), ''n.''   [Origin obscure.]   A perforated steel plate through which pipe or wire is drawn to reduce its diameter.   ''E. H. Knight.''

'''whish<sup>1</sup>''' (hwish), ''v. i.''   [Imitative; cf. ''whiz'' and ''swish.'']   To move with the whirring or whizzing sound of rapid motion.
{{smaller block|The scenery of a long tragic drama flashed through his mind as the lightning-express train ''whishes'' by a station.
{{right|''O. W. Holmes'', Professor, vi.}}}}

'''whish<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwish), ''interj.''   [Var. of ''hush.'']   Hush.
{{smaller block|<poem>What means this peevish babe? ''Whish'', lullaby;
What ails my babe? what ails my babe to cry?</poem>
{{right|''Quarles'', Emblems, ii. 8.}}}}

'''whish<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwish), ''a.''   [Var. of ''hush.'']   Silent: same as ''hush'', ''whisht'', ''whist''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|You took my answer well, and all was ''whish.''
{{right|''Sir J. Harington'', Ep., i. 27.}}}}

'''whishey, whishie''' (hwish′i), ''n.'' The whitethroat, ''Sylvia cinerea. Macgillivray.'' Also ''whattie.''

'''whisht†''' (hwisht), ''interj.'' and ''v.''   [Var. of ''husht.'']   Same as ''husht'', ''whist''<sup>1</sup>.
{{smaller block|When they perceived that Solomon, by the advise of his father, was annoynted king, by and by there was all ''whisht.''
{{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}}

'''whisk<sup>1</sup>''' (hwisk), ''n.''   [Prop. *''wisk''; < Icel. ''visk'', a wisp of hay, something to wipe with, a rubber, = Sw. ''viska'', a whisk, small broom, = Dan. ''visk'', a wisp, rubber, = D. ''wisch'' = OHG. ''wisc'', MHG. G. ''wisch'', a whisk, clout; prob. connected with ''wash''. The verb is from the orig. noun; but the noun in the later senses (‘act of whisking,’ etc.) is from the verb.]   '''1.''' A wisp or small bunch, as of grass, hair, or straw; specifically, such a wisp used as a brush, broom, or besom, and especially in modern usage one made of the ripened panicle of broom-corn (see ''broom-corn'' and ''Sorghum''), used for brushing the dust off clothes, etc.
{{smaller block|If you happen to break any china with the top of the ''whisk'' on the mantle-tree or the cabinet, gather up the fragments. {{right|''Swift'', Advice to Servants (Chamber-maid).}}}}
{{smaller block|The ceiling was divided by ''whisks'' of flowers, with a margin of honeysuckles. {{right|''S. Judd'', Margaret, ii. 11.}}}}
'''2.''' An instrument used for whisking, agitating, or beating certain articles, such as cream or eggs.—'''3.''' A coopers’ plane for leveling the chimes of casks.—'''4.''' A neckerchief worn by women in the seventeenth century. Also called ''falling-whisk'', apparently in distinction from the ruff.
{{smaller block|My wife in her new lace ''whiske'', which indeed is very noble, and I am much pleased with it. {{right|''Pepys'', Diary, II. 217.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>With ''whisks'' of lawn, by grannums wore,
In base contempt of bishops sleeves.</poem>
{{right|''Hudibras Redivivus'' (1706). (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''5.''' A brief, rapid sweeping motion as of something light; a sudden stroke, whiff, puff, or gale.
{{smaller block|<poem>This first sad ''whisk''
Takes off thy dukedom; thou art but an earl.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Noble Gentleman, v.}}}}
{{smaller block|He turned with an angry ''whisk'' on his heel, and swaggered with long strides out of the gate.
{{right|''J. S. Le Fanu'', Dragon Volant, iv.}}}}
{{smaller block|If a ''whisk'' of Fate’s broom snap your cobweb asunder.
{{right|''Lowell'', Blondel, ii.}}}}

'''6†.''' A servant. [Contemptuous.]
{{smaller block|This is the proud braches ''whiske''. {{right|''Brome'', Novella.}}}}

'''7.''' An impertinent fellow.   ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—'''Mexican''' or '''French whisk.''' {{smaller|Same as ''broom-root.''}}

'''whisk'''<sup>1</sup> (hwisk), ''v.''   [Prop. ''wisk'' (as in dial. use); < Sw. ''viska'', wipe, sponge, also wag the tail, = Dan. ''viske'', wipe, rub, sponge, = OHG. ''wisken'', MHG. G. ''wischen'', wipe, rub; from the noun.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To sweep or brush with a light, rapid motion: as, to ''whisk'' the dust from a table.
{{smaller block|She advanced to the fire, rearranged the wood, picked up stray brands, and ''whisked'' up the coals with a brush.
{{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, xxiv.}}}}

'''2.''' To agitate or mix with a light, rapid motion; beat: as, to ''whisk'' eggs.—'''3.''' To move with a quick, sweeping motion or flourish; move briskly.
{{smaller block|<poem>His papers light fly diverse, toss’d in air;
Songs, sonnets, epigrams the winds uplift,
And ''whisk'' ’em back to Evans, Young, and Swift.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, ii. 116.}}}} '''4.''' To flourish about.
{{smaller block|Who? he that walks in grey, ''whisking'' his riding-rod?
{{right|''Fletcher (and another)'', Noble Gentleman, ii. 1.}}}}
'''5.''' To carry suddenly and rapidly; whirl.
{{smaller block|The outsiders [in open railway-carriages], who experienced the inconvenience of the smoke as well as the cold atmosphere through which they were ''whisked''.
{{right|Quoted in ''First Year of a Silken Reign'', p. 150.}}}}
'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To move with a quick, sweeping motion; move nimbly and swiftly: as, to ''whisk'' away.
{{smaller block|<poem>Then, ill bested of counsel, rageth she [the Queen],
And ''whisketh'' through the town. ''Surrey'', Æneid, iv.</poem>}}
{{smaller block|I wish you would one day ''whisk'' over and look at Harley House.
{{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 44.}}}}

'''whisk<sup>2</sup>†''' (hwisk), ''n.''   [< ''whisk''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', referring, in the orig. form of the game called “''whisk'' and swabbers,” to the rapid action and the whisking or sweeping of the cards from the table as the tricks were won. There are various other card terms having reference to quick, sweeping action: e. g., ‘''sweep'' the stakes,’ ''slams'', etc. The name ''whisk'', having no very obvious significance after its first application, came to be called ''whist''. See ''whist''<sup>2</sup>.]   The game of whist.
{{smaller block|He plays at ''whisk'' and smokes his pipe eight-and-forty hours together sometimes.
{{right|''Farquhar'', Beaux’ Stratagem, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|He played at ''whisk'' till one in the morning.
{{right|''Walpole'', Letters, II. 417.}}}}

'''Whisk and swabbers.''' {{smaller|See ''swabber.''}}

'''whisker''' (hwis′kėr), ''n.''   [Formerly also (Sc.) ''whisquer, whiscar''; < ''whisk''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who or that which whisks, or moves with a quick, sweeping motion.—'''2.''' A switch or rod. [Old slang.]
{{smaller block|<poem>A whip is a ''whisker'' that will wrest out blood
Of back and of body, beaten right well.</poem>
{{right|''Harman'', Caveat for Cursetors, p. 122.}}}}
'''3.''' A bunch of feathers for sweeping anything.   ''Jamieson.''—'''4.''' In ''zoöl.'': (''a'') One of the long, stiff, bristly hairs which grow on the upper lip of the cat and many other animals; a vibrissa; a feeler; also, the set of such hairs on either side of the mouth. See ''vibrissa'', and cuts under ''Platyrhynchus'' and ''tiger.'' (''b'') ''pl.'' Any similar formation of hairs, feathers, etc., about an animal’s mouth; also, color-marks suggestive of whiskers, as mystacial or maxillary stripes. See ''whiskered.'' (''c'') In ''entom.'', a long fringe of hairs on the clypeus, overhanging the mouth, as in flies of the genus ''Asilus.''—'''5.''' The hair of the face, especially that on the sides of the face or cheeks of a man, as distinguished from that which grows on the upper lip (called the ''mustache'') and that on the chin (called the ''beard''), but the word was formerly also used for the hair on the upper lip: commonly in the plural. Compare ''side-whiskers.''
{{smaller block|His face not very great, ample forehead, yellowish reddish ''whiskers'', which naturally turned up; belowe he was shaved close, except a little tip under his lip.
{{right|''Aubrey'', Lives (Thomas Hobbes).}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>His ''whiskers'' curled, and shoe-strings tied,
A new Toledo by his side. ''Addison'', Rosamond, ii. 2.</poem> He had a beard too,. and ''whiskers'' turned upwards on his upper-lip, as lang as Baudron’s. {{right|''Scott'', Antiquary, ix.}}}}
{{smaller block|The Czar’s look, I own, was much brighter and brisker, But then he is sadly deficient in ''whisker''. {{right|''Byron'', Fragment of Epistle to Thomas Moore.}}}}
'''6.''' In ships, an outrigger of wood or iron extending laterally from each side of the bowsprit-cap, serving to support the jib and flying-jib guys.—'''7.''' Something great or extraordinary; a whopper; a big lie. ''Plautus made English'' (1694), p. 9. (''Davies.'')—'''8.''' A blusterer. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|March ''whisquer'' was never a good fisher. {{right|''Scotch proverb'' (Ray, Proverbs (1678), p. 385).}}}}

'''whiskerando''' (hwis-kẹ-ran′dō), ''n.''   [So called in allusion to ''Don Ferolo Whiskerandos'', a burlesque character in Sheridan’s play, “The Critic”: a name formed, with a Spanish-looking termination, < ''whisker''.]   A whiskered or bearded person. [Burlesque.]
{{smaller block|The dumpy, elderly, square-shouldered, squinting, carroty ''whiskerando'' of a warrior who was laying about him so savagely. {{right|''Thackeray'', Philip, xiii.}}}}

'''whiskerandoed†''' (hwis-kẹ-ran′dōd), ''a.''   [As ''whiskerando'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   Whiskered.
{{smaller block|To what follies and what extravagancies would the ''whiskerandoed'' macaronies of Bond Street and St. James’s proceed, if the beard once more were, instead of the neckcloth, to “make the man”! {{right|''Southey'', The Doctor, clvi.}}}}

'''whiskered''' (hwis′kėrd), ''a.''   [< ''whisker'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Wearing whiskers; having whiskers, in any sense.
{{smaller block|The ''whisker’d'' vermin race. {{right|''Grainger'', Sugar-Cane, ii.}}}}
{{smaller block|Again the ''whiskered'' Spaniard all the land with terror smote.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Belfry of Bruges.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
